reference_title: Design and Construction of Mechanically Stabilized Earth Walls and Reinforced Soil Slopes – Volume I

sections.title: Objectives
sections.body: This manual was prepared to assist design engineers, specification writers, estimators, construction inspectors and maintenance personnel with the selection, design, construction and maintenance of Mechanically Stabilized Earth Walls (MSEW) and Reinforced Soil Slopes (RSS). It is a comprehensive document integrating design, construction, materials, contracting, and monitoring aspects required for successful project implementation. The manual serves as FHWA's primary technical guideline on the use of these technologies on transportation facilities.
key_points: Covers MSE wall and RSS selection, design, construction, and maintenance
Addresses overview of MSE development, available systems, soil-reinforcement interaction, and design of routine and complex MSE walls
Covers design of MSE walls for extreme events, design detailing, steepened RSS design, specifications, contracting, and construction monitoring
A separate companion manual addresses long-term corrosion of metallic reinforcements and degradation of polymeric reinforcements
Includes design examples as appendices
sections.applicability: All MSE wall and reinforced soil slope projects on transportation facilities.

sections.title: Scope
sections.body: The manual addresses in a comprehensive manner: overview of MSE development and cost/advantages/disadvantages; available MSE systems and applications to transportation facilities; basic soil-reinforcement interaction; design of routine and complex MSE walls; design for extreme events; design detailing; design of steepened RSS; specifications and contracting approaches; construction monitoring and inspection; and design examples.
key_points: Covers both MSE walls (near-vertical face) and reinforced soil slopes (face inclination < 70 degrees)
Integrates all design, construction, materials, contracting, and monitoring aspects
Developed in support of FHWA educational programs
sections.applicability: Defines the scope of the two-volume manual.

sections.title: Source Documents
sections.body: This manual is an update of FHWA NHI-00-043 (Elias et al., 2001) and has evolved from AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications 4th Edition (2007) with 2008 and 2009 Interim Revisions; AASHTO LRFD Bridge Construction Specifications 2nd Edition (2004); Earth Retaining Structures FHWA-NHI-07-071; Geosynthetic Design and Construction Guidelines FHWA NHI-07-092; and earlier FHWA reinforced soil guidelines.
key_points: Primary design basis: AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications, 4th Edition 2007
Updated from FHWA NHI-00-043 (Elias et al., 2001)
Key companion references: FHWA-NHI-07-071 (Earth Retaining Structures), FHWA NHI-07-092 (Geosynthetics)
sections.applicability: Reference sources and lineage of the manual.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.body: Key terms used throughout the manual: Inclusion — generic term for all man-made elements incorporated in soil to improve behavior (steel strips, geotextile sheets, steel or polymeric grids, steel nails, tendons). Reinforcement — inclusions where soil-inclusion stress transfer occurs continuously along the inclusion. MSE Wall (MSEW) — generic term for reinforced soil with multiple reinforcement layers in placed fill. Reinforced Earth® is a trademark for a specific system. Reinforced Soil Slopes (RSS) — reinforced soil in constructed earth slopes with face inclinations less than 70 degrees. Geosynthetics — flexible polymeric materials (geotextiles, geomembranes, geonets, geogrids). Facing — component preventing soil raveling between reinforcement rows; common types include precast concrete panels, dry-cast modular blocks, gabions, welded wire mesh, shotcrete, timber lagging, and wrapped geosynthetics. Retained backfill — fill material behind the mechanically stabilized soil zone. Reinforced fill — fill material in which reinforcements are placed.
key_points: Inclusion is the generic term; reinforcement is the subset where continuous stress transfer occurs
MSE wall: near-vertical reinforced fill structure; RSS: reinforced slope with face < 70 degrees
Facing plays a minor structural role — primarily prevents raveling between reinforcement layers
Reinforced fill and retained backfill are distinct zones with different material requirements
sections.applicability: Definitions applicable throughout both volumes of GEC-11.

sections.title: Historical Development
sections.body: Inclusions to improve soil date to prehistoric times (straw in adobe bricks, sticks in mud dwellings, dikes of earth and tree branches used in China for 1,000+ years and along the Mississippi in the 1880s). Modern soil reinforcement for retaining walls was pioneered by French architect/engineer Henri Vidal in the early 1960s, leading to the invention of Reinforced Earth® using steel strip reinforcement. The first Reinforced Earth wall in the United States was built in 1972 on California State Highway 39. The highest permanent MSE wall in the U.S. is on the order of 150 ft (46 m). The first geotextile-reinforced wall was constructed in France in 1971 and in the United States in 1974. Geogrids for soil reinforcement were developed around 1980, with first use in earth reinforcement in 1981 and extensive U.S. use beginning about 1983. Currently, an estimated 9,000,000 ft2 (850,000 m2) of MSE retaining walls with precast facing are constructed per year in the United States, and 3,000,000 ft2 (280,000 m2) of modular block walls (MBW) per year. Available systems are listed in Tables 1-1 and 1-2.
key_points: Soil reinforcement dates to prehistoric times; modern MSE walls pioneered by Henri Vidal in early 1960s
First Reinforced Earth® wall in U.S.: 1972, California State Highway 39
Highest permanent U.S. MSE wall: ~150 ft (46 m) exposed height ~135 ft (41 m)
First geotextile wall: France 1971, U.S. 1974; first geogrid use: 1981
~9,000,000 ft2/yr precast-faced MSE walls and ~3,000,000 ft2/yr MBW walls constructed in U.S.
Most process patents have expired, leading to proliferation of systems and components
100-150 RSS projects constructed yearly in the U.S. with ~2,000,000 ft2/yr projected face area
sections.applicability: Historical context for MSE wall and RSS practice.

sections.title: Load and Resistance Factor Design (LRFD)
sections.body: The most significant update from the previous manual is the change from allowable stress design (ASD) to load and resistance factor design (LRFD) for MSE walls. FHWA and AASHTO established an October 1, 2010 deadline for implementation of LRFD in wall design. In ASD, all uncertainty in applied loads and material resistance are combined into a single factor of safety or allowable material stress. In LRFD, uncertainty in load and resistance are accounted for separately using load factors and resistance factors, where the resistance factor reflects the method used to estimate resistance (including model uncertainty). The AASHTO-LRFD framework has four limit states: (1) strength, (2) serviceability, (3) extreme event, and (4) fatigue. For most earth retaining system designs, strength or serviceability limit states control. Design for RSS structures remains based on limit equilibrium slope stability — AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications (2007) do not address RSS.
key_points: LRFD replaces ASD as of October 1, 2010 deadline (FHWA/AASHTO mandate)
LRFD separately accounts for load uncertainty (load factors) and resistance uncertainty (resistance factors)
Resistance factors are method-specific, capturing model uncertainty — key advantage over ASD
Four AASHTO LRFD limit states: strength, serviceability, extreme event, fatigue
Strength and serviceability limit states typically govern MSE wall design
RSS design remains limit equilibrium based — not addressed by AASHTO LRFD (2007)
AASHTO LRFD Section 11 covers earth retaining structures including MSE walls
AASHTO LRFD Section 10.4 covers evaluation of soil and rock properties for design
sections.applicability: Design framework for all MSE wall design in GEC-11; RSS design remains ASD/limit equilibrium.
